title: Multiplayer AI – Your Impending (And Accidental) Standard
summary: Multiplayer AI brings humans, AI, and “context” together into a persistent single place - and it's going to change where we work.
body_markdown:
## Where you do work is changing.


At the Dreamforce 2026 Slack keynote, Boris Cherny (the head of Anthropic’s Claude Code) approximated that 90% of his coding is done in Slack.


Why is he using a chat tool to code? And how?


Forgive the immediate use of a buzzword, but the answer to both questions is “multiplayer AI,” a slightly opaque term that’s simpler than you might expect.


The idea behind multiplayer AI is to bring humans, AI, and “context” together into a persistent single place for everyone to work together. “Context”, in this regard, includes conversation history, previously shared documents, permissions, organizational structure, prior decisions, active projects, etc. For more on context, please see Boris Evelson and Indranil Bandyopadhyay’s work:[The Next Evolution Of AI Will Rely On Context Layers](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-next-evolution-of-ai-will-rely-on-context-layers/?ref_search=3139934_1791380008426) .


Admittedly the name multiplayer AI is imperfect. “Multiplayer AI” can sound like several AI agents operating together. **But the defining feature of multiplayer AI is human participation.** If my colleagues and I are all working with an AI agent in a shared place (like a chat tool or even a Word doc) where everyone can see what AI – and others – are doing, ask AI or each other for help, and pick up with AI where a colleague left off, that’s multiplayer AI. Multiplayer AI can help facilitate agent-to-agent communications, but the most important part of is multiple humans interacting in a shared surface with AI.


### How does multiplayer AI work in practice?


In application development, to use Mr. Cherny as an example again: he leverages a Claude/Slack integration (Claude Tag) that allows Claude Code to live in Slack alongside Mr. Cherny and his team. Now, Claude can be dispatched to generate code and come back with an update in a shared chat thread, that everyone — Mr. Cherny, other users, or even other agents — can engage with.


And this doesn’t just apply to coding. Multiplayer AI is poised to transform collaborative work big and small. Instead of hunting through a dozen systems to find a data point, manually updating a client record, or constantly swiveling between a chat tool and creative suite to make 14 last-minute adjustments to an image, users can do all this work from a single place.


According to a sales development rep using multiplayer AI, they were spending 90% of their day in Slack and only spending 10% of their day in “singleplayer” interfaces.


### Why should I care about multiplayer AI now?


Beyond “it’s a thing,” why should you be thinking about (and planning for) multiplayer *now* ?


Well frankly, because multiplayer AI is going to be a standard way of working in the future. In fact, there’s a good chance this standardization will happen over the next year.


There are three forces driving this:


1. **Work is already *very* multiplayer today.** We humans spend a *lot* of time working with others. Employees report spending an average of 12 to 15 hours a week in meetings *(a day and a half).* This number doesn’t include “async collaboration” channels (email, chat, etc.) and often we’re collaborating with more than one person at the same time. Just think: How often are you on a video call with multiple people? In contrast, AI that’s trapped as an individual assistant cannot see enough of the team’s work to contribute effectively. AI right now is just adding another isolated interface that increases collaboration headache. AI needs broader collaboration capabilities and context to be useful. (By the way, an interesting side note that came out of the Hugging Face attack was OpenAI’s agents spontaneously created their own[message board](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/#~1200-agents-sent-%3E70,000-messages-and-files-on-an-unsanctioned-message-board,-and-~700-attacked-hugging-face) (by hijacking a package repository). They then used the appropriated filesystem to coordinate work, share notes and tools, and act as a persistent source of context as agents came and went. This is unexpectedly good proof that distributed sources of context will make agents jobs harder, and multi-agent systems will need *clear coordination channels* to actually manage more complex work. And it’s best if humans can ALSO be involved, instead of trusting a Minions-esque swarm of agents to go off and do work without adult supervision).
2. **Vendors are making multiplayer AI just kinda built in.** While Slack is eagerly embracing their role as a multiplayer AI shared surface (as evidenced by the recently launched[Slack Code](https://slack.com/features/code-channels) , Slackbot, and Salesforce’s headless strategy) it’s not just Anthropic and Slack doing this. Your shared surface of tomorrow could be a team chat tool, a shared document that allows multiple people to simultaneously edit, or some other “canvas” where people collaborate in real-time. Other vendors (in alphabetical order, non-exhaustive) like Asana, Atlassian (who recently introduced an[Agentic Multiplayer Protocol](https://atlassian.design/amp) ), ClickUp, Glean, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, ServiceNow, Zoom and more are championing and building multiplayer AI tools. As these come online, the trend of “it’s already there” from key tools will lead most organizations to accidentally adopt a multiplayer AI approach. Before this happens, I’d recommend testing multiplayer AI postures before it pops up suddenly in an unwelcome space because everyone *loves* spontaneously appearing chatbots (R.I.P. Clippy. You tried your best and I’ll always appreciate you for that).
3. **Our current way of working is horrifyingly inefficient (and organizations proved multiplayer AI works back in 2013).** Unfortunately, the way we work is bad. 86% of information worker decisionmakers reported using 4+ tools a week. 43% reported having to use 7+. It’s no wonder 46% of employees struggle finding critical information every month (or more often). Add collaboration fragmentation across email, chat, meetings, etc…, it’s a miracle we can work at all. And we know this is a problem. We’ve (kinda) already solved it before – back in 2013, with[ChatOps](https://www.forrester.com/report/Harness-ChatOps-To-Empower-Remote-Collaboration/RES153381?objectid=RES153381) , a direct forerunner. Then we did it again in the data space with[DataComs](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/right-insights-right-time-what-is-datacoms-and-why-should-you-care/) (2022), and[Curiosity Velocity](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/your-data-culture-is-doa/) (2023). The ideas behind each iteration are effectively identical to multiplayer AI: Turn shared chat interfaces into work hubs by extending them into multiple tools (systems of record or action) so people could automate and control work from Slack or eventually Teams. The issue was: This wasn’t universally accessible. You needed to know what an API was. With AI agents (and easier to connect to systems) this moat has effectively been bridged.


In short, multiplayer AI is needed to making AI useful to people, vendors are making it borderline a default, and it comes with the definitive benefit that it makes work less of a context switching nightmare. It’ll get introduced, and once it proves (once again) to make peoples lives better, it’ll stick.


So why wouldn’t someone want to work this way?


For some of what can go wrong (and how we can start to prepare our org) please see the forthcoming Part 2.
